Abyssinia. The ancient Christian empire in the Horn of Africa was known to the Greek world as Abyssinia, a name derived from Abyssinos meaning those from the depths. The nation officially adopted Ethiopia as its primary name during the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie, particularly after resisting Italian invasion in the nineteen-thirties. Ethiopia, taken from the Geez language of the region, means land of burnt faces, and it represents a reclamation of indigenous identity over Greek and European nomenclature.

The name Abyssinia itself comes from classical Greek terminology used by ancient and medieval geographers to describe the African highlands. Ethiopia, meanwhile, is one of the world's oldest Christian nations. It adopted Christianity as its state religion in the fourth century under Axumite rule, and this ancient faith has shaped its entire civilization. Haile Selassie, who ruled from eighteen-ninety-two to nineteen-seventy-five, was a reforming emperor who modernized Ethiopia and elevated its status during the League of Nations era.

When Italy invaded Ethiopia in nineteen-thirty-five under Mussolini, many thought the nation's independence would fall. But Emperor Haile Selassie rallied international support, and at the nineteen-thirty-six Battle of Adwa, Ethiopia emerged victorious, repelling the invasion. The nation officially began using Ethiopia in international forums during the nineteen-thirties through nineteen-fifties, and it became the standard designation after independence was confirmed.

What makes Ethiopia even more remarkable is that it was never fully colonized, unlike nearly every other African nation. This preservation allowed Ethiopia to maintain its ancient Geez script, its distinctive language, and its Orthodox Christian traditions. These connections to the Axumite empire, the Geez language, and the great reformer Haile Selassie all underscore how Ethiopia reclaimed its true name and its place in the world.
